title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page is a handwritten sheet slipped among Bourbaki-style typescript pages on Lie theory (n° 413). It contains two notes.

(1) The first note concerns moduli varieties of 'polarised, rigidified motives'. Typical examples are fine moduli spaces such as A_{g,n} with n ≥ 3, Shimura varieties, or quotients of period domains by a neat arithmetic group. Grothendieck records a property of such an M: a morphism f: X → M is determined by two pieces of data:
- its value f(x0) at a single point;
- the induced homomorphism π1(X,x0) → π1(M,f(x0)).

In modern terms this is a rigidity theorem.
- A map X → M is a polarised family of motives (Hodge structures, ℓ-adic systems) with rigidification over X.
- The π1-map fixes the underlying local system V.
- Given two such families with the same local system and the same fibre at x0, consider End(V). It underlies a polarisable variation of Hodge structure.
- The identity is a global flat section of End(V) that is of Hodge type (0,0) at x0. By Deligne's theorem of the fixed part it is then of type (0,0) everywhere, so the two Hodge filtrations coincide.
- For abelian schemes the same follows from Grothendieck–Mumford rigidity plus level structure.

Grothendieck calls this an important intrinsic property of M, one to be studied for its own sake (the object of 'étudiée pour ...' is uncertain). It is exactly the defining feature he later attributes to 'anabelian' varieties: maps are governed by π1 plus a point. He then conjectures a converse: perhaps varieties with this property can be interpreted as moduli varieties for certain types of motives.

(2) The second note proposes to 'introduce the notion of anabelian scheme'. 'Pointé' is crossed out and 'anabélien' inserted. Morphisms of such schemes should induce morphisms G(X,ξ) → G(Y,η) of some group object G(X,ξ). Its k-points (or fibre) recover the fundamental group: G(X,ξ)(k) = π1(X,ξ). This suggests a motivic or Galois-twisted fundamental group scheme (gerbe) attached to the pointed scheme, of which π1 is a realisation. The bubbled remark is illegible.

Purpose: to link the anabelian program (the section conjecture and Hom-conjecture in their pointed form) with motivic Galois theory via moduli of motives.
errors: The rigidity claim needs hypotheses: X connected and normal (e.g. smooth), M a fine moduli space (rigidification/level structure) of polarisable objects, and the π1-map taken with base points. Without these it fails. With them it is a correct consequence of the theorem of the fixed part (Hodge) or of rigidity of abelian schemes.

Note the contrast with non-rigid families (Faltings 1983): these deform with fixed monodromy but moving fibre at x0. So the 'value at a point' datum is genuinely necessary; it is not a counterexample.

The proposed converse (anabelian ⇒ moduli of motives) is speculative. Strict anabelian properties are known to fail for many Shimura varieties and other locally symmetric varieties of higher dimension, at least in the Hom-conjecture form; cf. the Ihara–Nakamura examples in higher dimension. So any such characterisation would have to be weakened.

ideas.what: A morphism X → M into a fine moduli space of polarised rigidified motives is determined by one value plus the π1-homomorphism
ideas.modern_name: Rigidity of variations of Hodge structure / theorem of the fixed part; rigidity of abelian schemes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Deligne (Théorie de Hodge II, 1971); Grothendieck/Mumford rigidity for abelian schemes (GIT 1965)
ideas.where_published: Rigidity of abelian schemes is in GIT (Mumford, crediting Grothendieck); the moduli-of-motives phrasing is unsure

ideas.what: Viewing this rigidity as the key intrinsic (anabelian-type) property of moduli varieties of motives, and conjecturing that varieties with it are moduli varieties for certain types of motives
ideas.modern_name: Anabelian property vs. period maps / Shafarevich-type conjectures; hyperbolicity of period domains
ideas.usually_credited_to: Anabelian ideas: Grothendieck (Esquisse 1984, letter to Faltings 1983); the VHS/hyperbolicity link is a diffuse later theme (Simpson, Zuo, Kollár)
ideas.where_published: Not as such. The Esquisse and the Faltings letter list moduli of curves (M_{g,n}) as anabelian, but do not propose that anabelian varieties are moduli of motives

ideas.what: Notion of anabelian (pointed) scheme whose morphisms induce maps of fundamental group objects G(X,ξ) → G(Y,η), with π1 = G(X,ξ)(k)
ideas.modern_name: Anabelian schemes; fundamental group scheme / Galois-twisted or motivic fundamental group as a group object over the motivic Galois group
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme; Letter to Faltings (1983) for anabelian schemes; the G(X,ξ) formalism is not published

missed.claim: Grothendieck explicitly identifies Hodge-theoretic rigidity of moduli of polarised rigidified motives as the anabelian property, and conjectures a converse: anabelian varieties might be moduli varieties for suitable classes of motives.
missed.quote: C'est une propriété intrinsèque importante de M ... Peut-être pourrait-elle être interprétée comme des variétés modulaires pour certains types de motifs.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: The anabelian literature (Nakamura, Tamagawa, Mochizuki, Hoshi) and the VHS/hyperbolicity literature (Shafarevich conjecture, Simpson's nonabelian Hodge theory, Zuo, Brunebarbe) developed largely separately. This page shows Grothendieck framing anabelian geometry as motivic moduli theory, a heuristic bridge that is not explicit in his published texts.

missed.claim: A sketched formalism in which anabelian schemes carry a group object G(X,ξ) — apparently a motivic or Galois-twisted fundamental group whose k-points are π1 — functorial in pointed morphisms.
missed.quote: Introduire la notion de schéma anabélien, et morphismes de tels, qui définissent des morphismes correspondants pour les G(X,ξ) → G(Y,η)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This prefigures a motivic or Tannakian formulation of the anabelian Hom-conjecture. Such formulations exist only partially in the literature (motivic π1 of Deligne; work comparing pro-unipotent/motivic and étale anabelian statements).

deep.surprise_reason: The rigidity statement itself is classical, and anabelian schemes are known from the Esquisse and the Faltings letter. However, the explicit proposal that anabelian varieties are moduli of motives, with rigidity of period maps as the anabelian property, is not in his circulated texts and is a modest but genuine unpublished heuristic.

Line 10: 'caractérisée' is struck through and 'interprétée(s)' written above; 'variétés' is inserted above a struck word.
The bubble near 'anabélien' reads something like '(c'est-à-dire des ... k)' and remains illegible; 'pointé' is the crossed-out word under 'anabélien'.
